status: Reviewed time, arithmetic and diagnostic precision corrections

changes.old: If the child says a week is longer than a month, show the month-grid holding several week-rows: 'Count the full weeks inside this month — there are four whole weeks, and most months have a few days left over.'
changes.new: If the child says a week is longer than a month, count the days: a Gregorian calendar month lasts 28–31 days, or four seven-day durations and zero to three extra days. Calendar week rows may cross month boundaries; they are not always four complete rows inside one month.

changes.old: Names the day after and before Wednesday without reciting from Sunday; places a month within the year (start/middle/end); uses the calendar to count on three days and names both the date and the weekday — showing days sit inside weeks inside months inside the year.
changes.new: Names the day after and before Wednesday without reciting from Sunday; places a month within the year; uses a calendar to count on three days and names both date and weekday. Relates days, weeks, months and years while recognising that a week can cross a month boundary.

changes.old: Do not reteach or confront this — the nested sense of time units firms up with age. Instead, build the nested structure visually — days inside a week-row, weeks inside a month-grid, months along a year-strip — and use ordering tasks ('which are shorter than a week?').
changes.new: Practise the related units visually: days in a week-row and calendar month, months along a year-strip. Show a week spanning two month pages; weeks are not required to fit exactly inside months. Compare durations with concrete dates rather than re-drilling the chant.

changes.old: Uses days and months functionally (any starting point, both directions), grasps the nesting (days in weeks in months in a year) and the cycle (the week/year repeats), and uses a calendar to locate and count dates.
changes.new: Uses days and months functionally from different starting points in both directions, relates their durations without treating every week as contained within one month, understands repeating weeks/years, and uses a calendar to locate and count dates.

changes.old: If the child keeps counting past the half hour ('40 past 3' for 3:40), point to the 12-6 partition: right is past, left is to, and 'to' times belong to the NEXT hour, so 3:40 is 'twenty to four'.
changes.new: Forty minutes past three and twenty minutes to four name the same time,3:40. Accept the equivalence; when practising conventional next-hour wording, ask the learner to count the 20 minutes remaining until four.

changes.old: '3:40' is 'twenty to four', not 'forty past three' — the minute hand is left of the 12-6 line, so name it against the next hour.
changes.new: 3:40 can be expressed equivalently as forty minutes past three or twenty minutes to four. Practise converting to the next-hour form when requested, rather than treating the equivalent elapsed-minutes reading as a wrong time.

changes.old: Answer discriminating questions such as 'Is 3:40 forty past three or twenty to four?'
changes.new: Express 3:40 as forty minutes past three and as twenty minutes to four, and explain why both locate the same time. Independently produce the requested next-hour form for a fresh example.

changes.old: Confuses times 'past' and 'to' — keeps counting past the half hour ('40 past 3' for 3:40) instead of switching to '20 to 4'
changes.new: Cannot convert a correct elapsed-minutes reading to the next-hour to-form when explicitly asked, or names the wrong next hour. Forty minutes past three is itself equivalent to 3:40, not a numerical misconception.

changes.old: Reads 3:40 as 'forty past three'; never flips to naming it against the next hour
changes.new: When asked for minutes remaining until the next hour at 3:40, cannot find 20 minutes to four or instead says twenty to three. Merely saying forty minutes past three does not establish a wrong time reading.

changes.old: Treats the hour as base-10 — writes a decimal point instead of a colon and/or thinks there are 100 minutes in an hour (so 50 past 3 = 50 to 4)
changes.new: Interprets the time separator as a decimal fraction or assumes 100 minutes per hour, for example saying 50 past 3 is 50 to 4. A full-stop time separator used conventionally is not itself this error; practise the requested colon format separately.

changes.old: Writes '3.25'; says 50 past 3 is 50 to 4
changes.new: Explains the minutes as hundredths of an hour or says 50 past 3 is 50 to 4. Writing 3.25 alone can be a conventional time notation and does not diagnose base-ten reasoning.

changes.old: Reads the numeral as the minutes, or reads a digital time literally with no past/to sense; assigns a.m./p.m. by feel; writes times with a decimal point.
changes.new: Reads the clock numeral as the minutes, cannot relate equivalent past/to readings, assigns a.m./p.m. by feel, or treats minutes as hundredths of an hour. A conventional full-stop separator alone is not a mathematical gap.

changes.old: If a learner gives a '35 past three' style answer for a left-side time, remind them they have crossed the bottom of the clock onto the 'to' side, and count the minutes back to the next hour (to four).
changes.new: Thirty-five minutes past three and twenty-five minutes to four are equivalent. Accept the time value, then ask for the next-hour to-form and count the 25 minutes remaining when practising that representation.

changes.old: Read twenty-five to four: minute hand on the 7, hour hand over halfway from 3 to 4 — and say why it is 'to four' and not '35 past three'.
changes.new: Read twenty-five to four with minute hand on 7 and hour hand over halfway from 3 to 4. Explain that it is the same time as thirty-five minutes past three; the to-form names the next hour and minutes remaining.

changes.old: After the half hour, keeps counting 'past' instead of switching to 'to' — reads twenty-five to four as 'thirty-five minutes past three'
changes.new: Cannot express a correct after-half-hour reading in the requested next-hour to-form. Thirty-five minutes past three correctly names the same time as twenty-five to four; assess whether the learner can translate between them when asked.

changes.old: Gives a '35 past' style answer for a left-side (to) time
changes.new: When explicitly asked how many minutes remain until four at 3:35, cannot determine 25 minutes or names the wrong next hour. A valid 35 past reading alone is not an error.

changes.old: Reads 'past' times to five minutes correctly, but keeps counting past after the half hour, confuses quarter to/past, or mislocates the hour hand for 'to' times.
changes.new: Reads past-times correctly but needs support to translate to a requested next-hour form, confuses quarter to with quarter past, or mislocates the hour hand. Accepts numerically equivalent past readings while assessing the required translation separately.

changes.old: 'If I move the hour hand to point exactly at the 7, is it still half past 7? What time is it now?'
changes.new: On a geared clock, wind back from half past seven until the hour hand points exactly at 7. Where is the minute hand now, and what time does the linked clock show? (Minute hand 12,7 o’clock.) Do not silently move only one independent hand and ask for a coherent new time.

changes.old: Reads 7:43 as 8:43 because the hour hand is near 8.
changes.new: If the learner reads 7:43 as 8:43 because the hour hand is near 8, trace back to the last hour passed:7. Keep the minutes 43 and check another face before concluding the hour-hand relation is secure.

changes.old: For 170+80, choose the correct result and explain why '15 tens' (a two-digit entry in the tens column) is wrong — ten of those tens must become a hundred (250).
changes.new: For 170 + 80, keep the original hundred visible: 170 is 1 hundred and 7 tens, and adding 8 tens yields 1 hundred and 15 tens, a valid unregrouped representation of 250. A compact H-T-O numeral cannot place 15 as one tens digit; exchange 10 tens for an additional hundred to write 2 hundreds and 5 tens, or 250.

changes.old: What's your evidence that 9 + 3 and 12 − 9 have the same answer?
changes.new: Why is the missing number in 9 + ? = 12 the same as the answer to 12 − 9? Show how both ask for the missing part.

changes.old: 403,072 and 'four hundred thousand and seven' both hinge on placeholder zeros, exposing period-reading and concatenation errors; the comparison 548,301/543,801 differs only at the thousands place, so a child scanning from the wrong end picks wrongly.
changes.new: 403,072 and 'four hundred thousand and seven' both hinge on placeholder zeros, exposing period-reading and concatenation errors; the comparison 548,301/543,801 has its first decisive difference at the thousands place (the hundreds digits also differ), so a child scanning from the wrong end picks wrongly.

changes.old: 3,472 vs 3,427 is judged by the ones/tens rather than the hundreds; ordering is scrambled.
changes.new: 3,472 vs 3,427 is judged by the ones (2 vs 7), rather than the first differing place, the tens (7 vs 2); thousands and hundreds tie.

changes.old: Compares by digit-count or a stray big digit; ordering ignores place value.
changes.new: Compares by a stray big digit or ignores the highest differing place; ordering ignores place value. Digit-count comparison itself is valid for non-negative whole numbers without leading zeros when linked to the extra highest place.

changes.old: Doesn't prioritise place value for magnitude — spreads the digit-sum evenly or fills low places, so the number isn't the largest (e.g. 333,300 or 111,138)
changes.new: Doesn't prioritise place value for magnitude — spreads the digit-sum evenly or fills low places, so the number isn't the largest (e.g. 333,330 or 111,138)

changes.old: Compares/orders large numbers by first digit or digit-count alone, misaligning place values
changes.new: Compares large numbers by an isolated digit or ignores the first differing place when lengths tie, misaligning place values. Comparing digit lengths is valid for non-negative whole numbers written without leading zeros.

changes.old: Orders 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 incorrectly, or calls a number with more digits automatically smaller/larger by looking at the wrong end.
changes.new: Orders 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 incorrectly, or compares same-length numbers from the wrong end. Correctly ordering this mixed-length trio by digit count is valid; ask for the corresponding highest-place explanation.

scope: Twenty-seven exact fields in ten saved guides. Valid equivalent time notations and number comparisons are not misconceptions; weeks can cross month boundaries; place-value subtotals distinguish unregrouped amounts from compact digits. No intrinsic criteria, age, context or dependency changes.
review: Independent reviewer completed assigned operative reads and peer-checked root nineteen time fields. Root checked the arithmetic and HTO context; the final retained-hundred clarification preserves the valid subtotal.
preservation: Every other guide field, all metadata/sourceClaims, intrinsic cards, alignments, source identities, dependencies and learner histories remain unchanged. No source Full promotion.
downstreamGate: Fresh private richer-research preservation and claim/consumer compatibility before staging; no reset or retrospective learner reinterpretation.
